_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: And that which is taught “liable,” where he was unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labors: for even if we hold that the intervening days are awareness, here one cannot say that the division of the Shabbatot is effective to divide [the two letters] so that they do not combine, since he holds that there is no awareness for a half-measure.
rashi:a4.1: Not in this one and not in that one: you cannot establish it as a case of unwittingness about the labors, since it was said above that for Rabbi Akiva [Shabbatot] are not like separate entities, and [the letters] combine; and not as unwittingness about Shabbat either, since even if we say that the intervening days are awareness to divide, we heard above of Rabban Gamliel that there is no awareness for a half-measure, as it teaches: in two lapses of awareness Rabban Gamliel deems him liable.
rashi:a6.1: Granted, if you say he holds in accordance with Rabbi Akiva: that Rabbi Akiva too holds that Shabbatot are like separate entities, and what it teaches, “concedes,” means he concedes to Rabbi Akiva, this is how they disagree: about one who writes one letter on this Shabbat and one letter on that Shabbat, unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labors. Rabban Gamliel deems him liable, as in the other baraita, since awareness on the intervening days is not effective for a half-measure; and Rabbi Akiva, who is the Rabbis who exempt, holds that there is awareness [for a half-measure].
rashi:a7.1: But if you say he holds in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer: in [a case of] unwittingness about the labors and intentional violation of Shabbat; for what it teaches, “and concedes,” it says about Rabbi Eliezer, so necessarily it is derived by inference that they disagree in part.
rashi:a8.1: Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable: he certainly says this about unwittingness about Shabbat, and that is why it teaches that there is no awareness for a half-measure. For if it were about unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labors [apparently meaning: intentional about Shabbat and unwitting about the labors], everyone agrees that according to Rabbi Eliezer Shabbatot are like separate entities and he is exempt.
rashi:a9.1: Rather, about one thread on a woven fabric: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer disagree, and this is what it says: Rabban Gamliel concedes to Rabbi Eliezer that one who writes one letter [on each of two Shabbatot], intentional about Shabbat and unwitting about the labor, is exempt, since Shabbatot are like separate entities, even though he disagrees with him about one thread on a woven fabric, where Rabban Gamliel deems him liable. And although that resembles this case of one who writes a half-measure on a second Shabbat and completes the measure begun on the first, since one who weaves [a single thread] onto the woven fabric also weaves a half-measure, even so Rabban Gamliel deems him liable. For here the reason is that Shabbatot are like separate entities and do not combine, which is like one who plows a half-measure and sows a half-measure; but in weaving, since from the outset there was a large measure woven in this garment, the thread he wove is counted together with the whole garment. And although the first tanna who disagrees with Rabban Gamliel about “there is no awareness for a half-measure” is not Rabbi Eliezer, even so this “and concedes” that it teaches refers to Rabbi Eliezer and to the dispute about one thread on a woven fabric; and the reason it is taught here together with the lapses of awareness is that it was discussing writing in halves. [The Gemara rejects this:] But Rabbi Eliezer too deems him liable!
rashi:a10.1: Rava said: Actually, the “concedes” that it teaches is a concession to Rabbi Eliezer, and it refers to this dispute: that they disagree about this one.
rashi:a10.2: In two lapses of awareness he is exempt: and there is awareness for a half-measure.
rashi:a10.3: To two domains: and both of them are public domains, he is exempt, since domains divide. In the baraita above, Rabban Gamliel concedes to Rabbi Eliezer that Shabbatot are like separate entities, which divide the writing of two letters so that they do not combine; but on this he disagrees with him, [holding] that domains do not divide.
rashi:a13.1: That is why he said to him, “Just as a menstruating woman”: since with a menstruating woman there is awareness on intervening days, as is explained below.
rashi:a14.1: But according to Rava, who says: that he asked him about [separate] entities, what does he resolve for him from a menstruating woman? With a menstruating woman, what division of entities is there?
rashi:a15.1: Teach “menstruating women”: just as with menstruating women, where there are not multiple results, one who has intercourse with five menstruating women is liable for each and every one, etc., since they are [separate] entities; is it not all the more so with Shabbatot, which are entities?
rashi:a15.2: Shmuel teaches “menstruating woman”: since he holds in accordance with Rav Ḥisda.
rashi:a19.1: Minor girls in general: many men who have intercourse with many minor girls who are menstruating.
rashi:a20.1: Not in accordance with this tanna: for this tanna holds that it was the menstruating woman that was his dilemma, while Shabbat was obvious to him.
rashi:a21.1: Liable for each and every one: if he performed five primary labors in one lapse of awareness.
rashi:a24.1: With an animal: many acts of intercourse with one [animal].
rashi:a24.2: The animal: it is a dilemma for him, like the menstruating woman.
rashi:a26.1: MISHNA: If there is uncertainty whether one ate forbidden fat: this is explained in the Gemara; one Sage says it is one piece and one Sage says two pieces.
rashi:a26.2: Or even if he ate: for example, he thought it was permitted fat, and afterward it became known to him that he ate forbidden fat, but it is uncertain whether there was an olive-bulk in it or not.
tosafot:a11.1: Rabban Gamliel is in accordance with the first tanna: and it is difficult: what does “in accordance with the first tanna” mean? For according to Rabban Gamliel, lapses of awareness do not divide, and according to its plain sense we cannot say this, since the first tanna said that in two lapses of awareness he is exempt.
tosafot:a24.1: He said to him: One who copulates with an animal will prove it, as there are no separate entities: the same is true that he could have said “a menstruating woman will prove it,” since Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable for each and every one; but he had not heard [a ruling about] a menstruating woman from his teachers, only about an animal, so he cited that.
tosafot:a26.1: MISHNA: If there is uncertainty whether one ate, etc.: it is referring to a case where, at the time he ate, he thought it was permitted fat. For if he knew it was possibly forbidden fat, how could he bring an offering? He would not have turned back on account of his knowledge [and an offering comes only for one who would have refrained had he known].
gershom:a1.1: And that which is taught “liable,” where unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labors: for the intervening days are awareness to divide, and he holds that here it is not awareness to divide, since there is no awareness for a half-measure; rather, they combine and he is liable.
gershom:a2.1: But according to Rava, who says Rabbi Akiva holds that Shabbat is like one entity: for this is what Rava said above: [Rabbi Eliezer] resolved for him that they are like separate entities, and he did not accept it from him, but held that they are like one entity.
gershom:a3.1: Granted, that which is taught “liable,” you find it both where intentional about Shabbat and unwitting about the labors, for that is the reason he is liable, that Shabbatot are like one entity; and where unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labors, that the intervening days are awareness, and here he is liable, since there is no awareness for a half-measure, and they combine.
gershom:a4.1: But that which is taught “exempt,” in what case do you establish it? Not in this one and not in that one: not where intentional about Shabbat and unwitting about the labors, and not where unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labors.
gershom:a5.1: Rava could say to you: you cannot derive [anything] from here, for I say that Rabban Gamliel, who exempts, holds in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, who said in the mishna that Shabbatot are like separate entities; therefore the Shabbatot do not combine. And he does not hold in accordance with Rabbi Akiva.
gershom:a6.1: But from the fact that it teaches here, “and Rabban Gamliel concedes,” [by inference] they disagree about another [case]: Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis.
gershom:a7.1: Granted, if you say: this “and Rabban Gamliel concedes to the Rabbis,” where the Rabbis are Rabbi Akiva, that Rabban Gamliel holds in accordance with Rabbi Akiva:
gershom:a8.1: This is how they disagree: about another [case], where unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labors, that the intervening days are awareness to divide.
gershom:a9.1: For Rabban Gamliel holds there is no awareness for a half-measure: and he is liable.
gershom:a11.1: And Rabban Gamliel concedes to Rabbi Akiva where intentional about Shabbat, etc. But if you say Rabban Gamliel holds in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, where Rabbi Eliezer is the Rabbis that it mentions and Rabban Gamliel concedes to them, by inference they disagree about another [case]; about what do they disagree?
gershom:a12.1: If where unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labor: that the intervening days are awareness to divide, and Rabban Gamliel, who deems him liable, holds that there is no awareness for a half-measure; in this even Rabbi Eliezer holds in accordance with Rabban Gamliel that there is no awareness for a half-measure.
gershom:a13.1: As it is taught: One who writes two letters, etc., Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable. And rather, Rabbi Eliezer disagrees about one thread on a woven fabric? That too is a half-measure, and in that too Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable.
gershom:a14.1: As we learned: Rabbi Eliezer says: One who weaves, etc. Rather, [Rabban Gamliel] certainly holds in accordance with Rabbi Akiva. Rava said: Actually, he holds in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, and by inference they disagree about this one.
gershom:a15.1: As we learned: One who carried out half a dried fig and then carried out half a dried fig in one lapse of awareness is liable: since they combine.
gershom:a16.1: In two lapses of awareness: he is exempt.
gershom:a17.1: Rabbi Yosei says: In one lapse of awareness, if he carried them out to one domain he is liable, since they combine; to two domains they do not combine and he is exempt. Rabban Gamliel is stringent in accordance with the first tanna, and holds that in one lapse of awareness he is liable even though he carried them out to two domains; and Rabbi Eliezer holds in accordance with Rabbi Yosei, that if he carried them out to two domains he is exempt, even though it was in one lapse of awareness. And this is what they disagree about. [Next the Gemara asks:] in these [matters], is it more reasonable [to explain] in accordance with Rava or with Rav Ḥisda?
gershom:a18.1: Rabbi Eliezer said to him: He is liable for each and every one, a fortiori: Just as a menstruating woman, etc.
gershom:a19.1: Granted, according to Rav Ḥisda, who says unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about the labor: where there is no division of labors, and he asked him whether the intervening days are awareness to divide or not.
gershom:a20.1: That is why he said to him, “Just as a menstruating woman”: for there too, with a menstruating woman, the intervening days are awareness to divide, as is explained below.
gershom:a21.1: But according to Rava, etc.: that he asked him whether they are like separate entities or not, and he said to him “just as a menstruating woman,” which is one entity? If so, he should have taught “just as menstruating women,” since menstruating women are separate entities.
gershom:a22.1: Rava could say to you: Teach “just as menstruating women.” Shmuel teaches “menstruating woman,” and he holds in accordance with Rav Ḥisda.
gershom:a23.1: And according to Rav Ḥisda: a menstruating woman, what intervening days that are awareness to divide does she have? Rava said: For example, where he had intercourse with her and she immersed, etc.: for the immersions are like intervening days, to divide each act of intercourse.
gershom:a24.1: Granted, according to Rava, who says he asked him whether Shabbat is like separate entities or not, that is why it teaches “one who has intercourse with minor girls,” who are separate entities.
gershom:a25.1: But according to Rav Ḥisda, who says he asked him whether the intervening days are awareness to divide:
gershom:a26.1: Why does it say “one who has intercourse with minor girls”? Let it teach “one who has intercourse with a minor girl five times,” for she has intervening days to divide, as we said.
gershom:a27.1: Indeed, it could have taught that; and what is “minor girls”? All minor girls in general: if he had intercourse with one of them many times, he is liable for each and every one.
gershom:a28.1: The mishna is not in accordance with this tanna, as it is taught: Rabbi Shimon said, etc. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads “Rabbi Shimon”; the daf reads Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.]
gershom:a29.1: Shall you say the same of a menstruating woman, with regard to whom there are not multiple results: many matters, neither primary categories nor subcategories, only the single liability for intercourse. No, if you said it of minor menstruating girls, who are separate entities, shall you say it of a menstruating woman, who is one entity?
gershom:a30.1: He said to him: One who copulates with an animal will prove it. He said to him: The animal, since it is one entity, is a dilemma for me just like the menstruating woman: whether he is liable only once or for each and every one.
gershom:a32.1: If there is uncertainty whether one ate forbidden fat, etc.
rashi:b2.1: He ate one of them: and he thought it was permitted fat, and afterward it became known that one was forbidden fat, and he does not know which he ate; he brings a provisional guilt offering. But if at the time of eating he was in doubt and acted intentionally, eating it despite the doubt, he is an intentional sinner and is exempt.
rashi:b2.2: He unwittingly engaged in intercourse with one of them: he thought this was his wife, and afterward he was in doubt which of them it was; he brings a provisional guilt offering. And if it became known to him that it was his sister, he brings a sin offering.
rashi:b3.1: So too, where their status is unknown: for example, he ate two pieces thinking they were permitted fat, and afterward it became known that they were uncertain; he brings only one provisional guilt offering, since it did not become known to him between one eating and the next that he had possibly eaten forbidden fat.
rashi:b4.1: If he had knowledge in between: knowledge of the uncertainty.
rashi:b4.2: Just as he brings a sin offering for each and every one: if there was certain knowledge in between.
rashi:b4.3: So too: with knowledge of the uncertainty he brings two provisional guilt offerings.
rashi:b6.1: GEMARA: We learned one piece: he ate one piece thinking it was permitted fat, and afterward it became known to him that it was uncertain. This is what the mishna teaches: “If there is uncertainty whether one ate forbidden fat,” etc.
rashi:b6.2: A piece out of two pieces: as is explained in the latter clause, “permitted fat and forbidden fat were before him,” etc. But for one piece he is exempt.
rashi:b7.1: Mitzvat is written: in Leviticus, regarding the provisional guilt offering: “And does any of the mitzvot of the Lord that are not to be done, and does not know it, yet he is guilty, and shall bear his iniquity; and he shall bring his guilt offering,” etc. [Leviticus 5:17–18].
rashi:b8.1: We read mitzvot: which implies one out of two.
rashi:b10.1: Need it be said of two pieces?: for granted, with one piece there is room to distinguish, for the reason given below, that it is impossible to identify its prohibition, or that its prohibition was not established; but with two pieces one cannot say so.
rashi:b14.1: Koy: uncertain whether it is a domesticated animal or a non-domesticated animal.
rashi:b14.2: A provisional guilt offering: even though there is no piece out of two pieces, if he ate its fat unwittingly, thinking it was a non-domesticated animal.
rashi:b16.1: Uncertain whether nine months old, etc.: the yevama who entered levirate marriage within three months [of her husband’s death].
rashi:b17.1: And they are obligated to bring a provisional guilt offering: perhaps it is the son of the first [husband], and it turns out that he had intercourse with his brother’s wife who has children, which is [punishable] by karet. And this woman is comparable to one piece.
rashi:b18.1: Found on his: in Tractate Nidda, in the chapter Kol HaYad (Nidda 14a): it is the way of Jewish women to engage in intercourse with two cloths, one for him and one for her, to wipe with. If it was found on his, it was certainly at the time of intercourse, and he had intercourse with a menstruating woman unwittingly, and they are liable to two sin offerings.
rashi:b19.1: Otyom: it is a Greek word, meaning: [immediately] after intercourse.
rashi:b19.2: After time: there [in Nidda] its measure is explained.
rashi:b19.3: And they are liable to a provisional guilt offering: but why? There are not two mitzvot.
rashi:b21.1: It is possible to identify its prohibition: for a provisional guilt offering comes only to shield from suffering until it becomes known to him and he brings a sin offering, as is explained in the last chapter (below, Keritot 25a). Therefore, with two pieces, [where he ate one] and the other remained, it is possible that an expert will come later and recognize whether the remaining one is permitted fat; [if it is,] he certainly ate forbidden fat, and he will bring a sin offering. But one piece that he ate cannot be identified.
rashi:b22.1: What is there between Rava: who said above that Rav’s reason is because the vocalization is authoritative.
rashi:b22.2: And Rabbi Zeira: who explains Rav’s reason as identifying its prohibition.
rashi:b22.3: This is the reading: “The difference between them is an olive-bulk and a half”: for example, two pieces, in one an olive-bulk and in the other half an olive-bulk, and he ate the one of an olive-bulk, and it is not known whether it is forbidden fat or permitted fat.
rashi:b23.1: According to Rava there are not mitzvot: there are not two olive-bulks, and less than an olive-bulk is as though it does not exist.
rashi:b23.2: According to Rabbi Zeira it is possible to identify the prohibition: with this half olive-bulk that remains.
rashi:b24.1: A koy, they are obligated, etc.: but it is impossible to identify its prohibition!
tosafot:b9.1: From the fact that the latter clause is two pieces, the first clause too is two pieces: and that [clause] too, “or even if he ate and it is uncertain whether there was the measure in it,” etc., must likewise be referring to where there are two pieces before him and both of them have the measure. And one must necessarily say so, since we say below, “The difference between them is an olive-bulk and a half,” that according to the one who says [the reason is that] the prohibition was established, there is none [i.e., no obligation]; if so, learn from it that there are two pieces. And in any case he ate this olive-bulk, and even if he ate from the forbidden one, he is uncertain whether he ate an olive-bulk; and it teaches us that even for a double uncertainty he brings a provisional guilt offering. And with Shabbat and a weekday, too, we can find two pieces: for example, he performed labor at twilight, which is uncertain day or night; and the prohibition was also established, as he performed labor at twilight near the conclusion of Shabbat, when the prohibition was established all day; and it is also possible to identify the prohibition, since one can see from the nature of the labor he performed, relative to how much of the night has passed: if only a little of it has passed and he performed a great deal of labor, then he performed some of it during the day.
tosafot:b12.1: Rav Yehuda says that Rav says, etc., one piece, he is exempt, etc.: And if you say: but we say in the second chapter of Ketubot (22b), regarding “two say he died and two say he did not die,” etc., and the Gemara asks there: one who has intercourse with her stands to bring a provisional guilt offering. But what is the difficulty? We require mitzvot! One may answer that there the difficulty is raised according to the one who says here that we do not require a piece out of two pieces. But it is difficult, Rav against Rav: for here it says “Rav Yehuda says that Rav says,” and in the chapter HaIsha Rabba (Yevamot 88a) it says, “Rabba says that Rav says: They taught this only where she married on the testimony of one witness,” etc., and the Gemara asks: one who has intercourse with her stands to bring a provisional guilt offering. But what is the difficulty? And one answers that this is the difficulty: one who has intercourse with her stands in a prohibition that entails a provisional guilt offering. And further, one may answer that there the difficulty is raised according to Rav Naḥman, who explains Rav’s reason here as because the prohibition was established, so that where a gentile ate the first [piece] and he ate the second, he is liable, since the prohibition was established. And there it fits well that the difficulty is properly raised, since it was already established that she was a married woman.
tosafot:b14.1: Abaye raised an objection: all these refutations he could have raised above against Ḥiyya bar Rav.
tosafot:b19.1: And it is taught with regard to it: And they are liable to a provisional guilt offering. And it is difficult: for here it implies that the baraita explains the mishna, while there, in the chapter Kol HaYad (Nidda 14b), it does not imply this, for it says on the mishna’s “and they are exempt from the offering”: it was taught, “and they are liable to a provisional guilt offering,” and our tanna holds that we require a piece out of two pieces. And further, it is somewhat difficult: why does it not say [object] from this (Horayot 8b): “And they bring a provisional guilt offering for a positive commandment and for a prohibition concerning a menstruating woman,” even though there are not two pieces?
gershom:b1.1: [This note continues 17a in Rabbeinu Gershom’s arrangement.] He brings a provisional guilt offering for any uncertainty among these, and when it becomes known to him that he certainly ate, he brings a sin offering. So too, for their unknown status, where it did not become known to him that he certainly ate but it became known to him that he possibly ate forbidden fat, he brings only one provisional guilt offering.
gershom:b2.1: If he had knowledge in between: between one olive-bulk and the next. Just as with certain knowledge he brings a sin offering for each one, so with knowledge of the uncertainty he brings a provisional guilt offering for each and every one.
gershom:b3.1: Just as where he ate forbidden fat, blood, notar and piggul in one lapse of awareness, having no awareness until the end, he is liable to a sin offering for each and every one, since they are distinct categories:
gershom:b4.1: So too for their unknown status: where it became known to him that he possibly ate forbidden fat, blood and notar, he brings a provisional guilt offering for each one.
gershom:b5.1: We learned one piece: in the first clause of the mishna.
gershom:b6.1: And Ḥiyya bar Rav said: We learned one piece out of two pieces: one of forbidden fat and one of permitted fat, where he does not know which he ate.
gershom:b7.1: With regard to what do they disagree? After all, according to both Sages he is liable to a provisional guilt offering; about what do they disagree?
gershom:b8.1: Rav Asi holds that the tradition [of spelling] is authoritative; mitzvat is written: “And if any one soul sins unwittingly from the people of the land, in doing any of the mitzvat of the Lord that are not to be done” [Leviticus 4:27]. That is one piece, uncertain forbidden fat or uncertain permitted fat, which one is commanded not to eat.
gershom:b9.1: The vocalization is authoritative; we read mitzvot: that is, two pieces of uncertain status, which one is commanded not to eat.
gershom:b10.1: Do not go after the opposite: do not turn [the argument] around after objections; he can answer you, etc.
gershom:b11.1: Until he is unwitting with regard to two mitzvot: with two pieces, since he holds that the vocalization is authoritative and we read mitzvot.
gershom:b12.1: Koy: about which the Sages did not decide whether it is a species of non-domesticated animal or of domesticated animal; one is liable to a provisional guilt offering for its fat. But a koy is one piece!
gershom:b13.1: He said to him: Rabbi Elazar [the daf reads Rabbi Eliezer] holds that the tradition [of spelling] is authoritative; mitzvat is written.
gershom:b14.1: Uncertain whether nine months old, of the first: for example, one who had intercourse with his yevama within three months of his brother’s death, and the wife gave birth at the end of six months, and it is uncertain whether it is nine months old and of the first, or seven months old and of the latter. He must divorce her, since perhaps the child is the son of the first, so she was not bound to him [in levirate], and he transgressed with her the prohibition of a brother’s wife. And the child is unflawed either way: if it is the son of the first, it is unflawed, and if it is the son of the latter, it is unflawed.
gershom:b15.1: And they are liable: both of them, to a provisional guilt offering, since neither he nor she knew that she was pregnant. But this woman is one piece, and it teaches that they are liable to a provisional guilt offering.
gershom:b16.1: This too is Rabbi Elazar [the daf reads Rabbi Eliezer], who holds that the tradition is authoritative.
gershom:b17.1: Found on his, they are impure and liable to an offering: for we say that Jewish women engage in intercourse with two cloths; after intercourse they examine themselves to see whether they are pure, one for him and one for her. With one cloth she wipes her husband, to see whether there is any blood on the cloth, and with one cloth she wipes herself. If blood was found on his cloth, they are impure, since it is known that at the time of intercourse she was menstruating; and all the pure items they touched from then on are impure; and they are liable to a sin offering for the menstruating woman, since they were unwitting. And likewise if blood was found on her cloth.
gershom:b18.1: Otyom [spelled differently in Rabbeinu Gershom’s text]: meaning immediately after intercourse; they are also impure and liable to an offering, since it is known that at the time of intercourse she was menstruating.
gershom:b19.1: Found on her cloth after time: after he had intercourse with her; for example, she did not examine herself immediately after intercourse but after some time, and found blood. They are impure due to uncertainty, since it is uncertain whether she was menstruating at the time of intercourse, or perhaps she saw [blood] afterward. Therefore they are impure due to uncertainty, and all the pure items they touched, retroactively from the time of intercourse, are held in suspense: they are neither eaten nor burned.
gershom:b20.1: And exempt from the offering: from a sin offering.
gershom:b21.1: And it is taught with regard to it: And they are liable to a provisional guilt offering. But this woman is one piece, and it teaches that they are liable to a provisional guilt offering.
gershom:b22.1: One piece, uncertain forbidden fat and uncertain permitted fat, and he ate it, he is exempt: entirely. What is Rav’s reason? He holds: two pieces, one of forbidden fat and one of permitted fat, therefore he is liable to a provisional guilt offering, since with two pieces it is possible to identify their prohibition, whether he touched and ate the actual prohibited item. For they examine the other that remained: one who is an expert can see whether this one is permitted fat, [and then] the one he ate was certainly forbidden fat. Therefore, before they have examined it, they are liable to a provisional guilt offering; and after they have examined it and it became known to him that it was certainly forbidden fat, he is liable to a sin offering. But one piece, uncertain forbidden fat and uncertain permitted fat, that he ate: once he has eaten it, it is impossible to identify the prohibition, whether it was forbidden fat or permitted fat; therefore he does not bring a provisional guilt offering, since a provisional guilt offering is brought only for a matter that can be clarified later. There are those who say: with two pieces it is possible to identify the prohibition, therefore he is liable, since he should have clarified which one he ate; but with one piece, what can he clarify about it? Therefore he is exempt.
gershom:b23.1: What is the difference between the reason of Rabba [the daf reads Rava] and the reason of Rabbi Zeira? Both of them require one piece out of two pieces. The difference between them is an olive-bulk and a half: for example, two pieces, one with an olive-bulk and one with half an olive-bulk, and it is not known which is forbidden fat, and he ate the one with an olive-bulk.
gershom:b24.1: According to Rabba there are mitzvot: for in any case there are two pieces. [This first version runs opposite to the daf, which says that according to Rava there are not mitzvot; the daf’s reading is the “other version” in the next note.]
gershom:b25.1: According to Rabbi Zeira it is impossible to identify its prohibition: for the half olive-bulk that remained is not recognizable as forbidden fat or permitted fat, since it is a small amount; therefore he is exempt. Another version: according to Rabba there are not mitzvot, since mitzvot implies two whole pieces, and there are not, and he is exempt. According to Rabbi Zeira he is liable, since with the half olive-bulk too it is possible to identify its prohibition, whether it is permitted fat or forbidden fat, by one who is an expert, with difficulty, to know what the whole olive-bulk was; therefore it is like two pieces, and he is liable.
gershom:b26.1: Rabbi Yirmeya raised an objection to Rabbi Zeira, for, etc.: and [from] the uncertain nine-month child, and the menstruating woman where [blood] was found on her [cloth] after time; in all these it is impossible to identify their prohibition, and yet they are liable to a provisional guilt offering. And he resolved it for him regarding all of them: [Sefaria’s text marks the end of the part on 17b here.] In accordance with whose opinion is this? It is Rabbi Elazar [the daf reads Rabbi Eliezer], and not the opinion of all.
